reference.source: Resnick's Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: Part of the X-linked otopalatodigital spectrum caused by gain-of-function variants in FLNA, encoding the actin-cross-linking protein filamin A
Characteristic craniofacial features include a prominent supraorbital ridge with a heavy bony brow, hypertelorism and a small jaw with dental anomalies
The skeleton shows metaphyseal undermodelling (an Erlenmeyer-flask tendency), progressive scoliosis, joint contractures and hand and foot anomalies
Conductive and mixed hearing loss is common owing to ossicular and middle-ear involvement
As an X-linked condition, males are generally more severely affected than heterozygous females, who show milder and more variable features
Extraskeletal features such as urogenital and airway anomalies may occur across the FLNA otopalatodigital spectrum
Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, with hearing surveillance and support, orthopaedic care for scoliosis and contractures, and monitoring for cranial-nerve foraminal narrowing
reference.pathophysiology: Frontometaphyseal dysplasia is caused by gain-of-function variants in FLNA, an X-linked gene encoding filamin A, a cytoskeletal protein that cross-links actin filaments and coordinates cell shape, migration and mechanotransduction. Altered filamin A function disturbs the modelling and remodelling of the skeleton, producing the prominent frontal bony ridge, metaphyseal undermodelling, contractures and progressive spinal deformity. Involvement of the ossicles and middle ear underlies the hearing loss. Because FLNA is X-linked, hemizygous males typically manifest a more severe phenotype, while heterozygous females are protected to a variable degree by X-inactivation, producing the characteristic sex difference across the otopalatodigital spectrum.
additionalDifferentials: Osteodysplasty and other skeletal dysplasias with metaphyseal flaring
Larsen syndrome and other contracture-associated dysplasias
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal survey demonstrating the supraorbital ridge, metaphyseal undermodelling and hand and foot anomalies
Spinal imaging to detect and monitor scoliosis
Audiometry and middle-ear assessment for conductive or mixed hearing loss
Skull imaging to assess for foraminal narrowing where cranial-nerve symptoms arise
FLNA molecular genetic testing with X-linked segregation analysis
Urogenital and airway evaluation given the broader FLNA spectrum
redFlags: Progressive scoliosis causing respiratory or neurological compromise
Airway obstruction or laryngotracheal narrowing in the FLNA spectrum
reference.prognosis: The prognosis depends on severity and sex, with males often more significantly affected; intelligence is usually normal and life expectancy generally preserved, though scoliosis, contractures, hearing loss and airway or urogenital anomalies contribute to morbidity.
pitfalls: Failing to recognise the disorder as part of the FLNA otopalatodigital spectrum and its X-linked inheritance
Overlooking hearing loss and delaying audiological support
Missing progressive scoliosis that requires timely orthopaedic management
Underestimating extraskeletal (urogenital or airway) involvement within the spectrum
references: Resnick's Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders
management: Audiological management of conductive and mixed hearing loss with hearing aids and otological surgery for ossicular involvement
Orthopaedic and physiotherapy management of progressive scoliosis, joint contractures and hand and foot anomalies, with bracing or surgery
Surveillance for foraminal narrowing and cranial-nerve compromise, with neurosurgical assessment where symptoms arise
Evaluation and management of urogenital and airway anomalies across the FLNA otopalatodigital spectrum
Regular monitoring of spinal deformity, hearing and skeletal progression
Multidisciplinary coordination across metabolic bone, clinical genetics, ENT, orthopaedics and dentistry
Genetic counselling for the X-linked FLNA disorder, noting greater severity in males, with carrier testing and recurrence-risk discussion
